title: Contra Cresconium
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa019.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Sed, credo, cum me uideres a nonnullis putari eloquentem, ut a me lectoris auditorisue studium deterreres, accusandam existimasti eloquentiam, ut iam quid dicerem non adtenderet, quisquis abs te perterritus tamquam eloquenter me dicentem eo ipso iam cauendum fugiendumque censeret. nide ergo, ne hoc quod fecisti sit artis illius malae, quam, sicut de Platone commemorasti, nonnulli recte iudicauerunt de ciuitate ac de humani generis societate pellendam. haec non est eloquentia — quae utinam mihi ad explicanda ea quae sentio pro desiderio prouenisset! —, sed quaedam sophistica et maligna professio, quae sibi proponit non ex animo, sed ex contentione uel commodo pro omnibus et contra omnia dicere. de hac ait sancta scriptura: qui sophistice loquitur odibilis est; ab hac mihi uidetur Paulus apostolus iuuentutem Timothei prohibere, ubi ait: noli uerbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est nisi ad subuersionem audientium. et ne a facultate recte dicendi eum prohibuisse putaretur, continuo subiecit: satis age te ipsum probabilem operarium exhibere deo non erubescentem, uerbum ueritatis recte tractantem. nimirum itaque tibi haec animi subrepsit affectio, quod contradicendi studio, non quo ita sentires, sed quo a nobis intentionem discere uolentis auerteres, perhibuisti nos eloquentes et uituperasti eloquentiam.
passages.english: But, I suppose, since you saw that I am thought eloquent by some, in order to deter the eagerness of a reader or hearer from me you judged that eloquence should be accused, so that whoever was frightened off by you would no longer attend to what I said, but would consider that I, as one speaking eloquently, was for that very reason to be guarded against and avoided. See, then, that what you have done does not belong to that evil art which, as you recalled about Plato, some have rightly judged should be driven out of the city and out of the fellowship of the human race. This is not eloquence — would that it had come to me as fully as I desire for setting out what I think! — but a certain sophistical and malicious profession, which sets itself to speak for all things and against all things, not from conviction but from contentiousness or for advantage. Of this holy scripture says: "He who speaks sophistically is hateful"; from this, it seems to me, the apostle Paul restrains the youth of Timothy, where he says: "Do not contend about words; for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of the hearers." And so that he should not be thought to have restrained him from the capacity of speaking rightly, he immediately added: "Strive to present yourself to God as an approved workman, not ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth." Clearly, then, this disposition of mind crept up on you: that out of zeal for contradiction, not because you thought so, but in order to turn away from us the attention of one wishing to learn, you declared us eloquent and found fault with eloquence.

passages.original: quod tamen ad quaestionem quam nunc discutimus sufficit, adtende, obsecro te, Hebraeum ex Hebraeis apostolum Christi stantem ac sermocinantem non in synagoga Iudaeorum neque in ecclesia christianorum, sed in Areopago Atheniensium, hoc est contentiosorum maxime impiorumque Graecorum. ibi enim loquacissimae philosophorum haereses extiterunt. quarum nonnullae, sicut ipsi qui hic commemorati sunt Stoici, magis de uerborum quam de rerum aduersitate confligunt, quod apostolus prohibuit Timotheum, dicens ad nihil esse utile nisi ad subuersionem audientium. nam de his, ut nosti, Tullius ait: uerbi enim controuersia iam diu torquet homines Graeculos, contentionis cupidiores quam ueritatis. hos tamen Paulus noster adloquendos corrigendosque suscepit nec ipsius loci nomine exterritus, quod ex Marte inditum resonat, quem deum dicunt esse bellorum, ibi pacifica credituris intrepidus loquebatur, ibi spiritalibus adcinctus annis perniciosos expugnabat errores nec contentiosos tamquam mitissimus nec dialecticos tamquam simplicissimus formidabat.
passages.english: Yet, as far as suffices for the question we are now discussing, consider, I beg you, the apostle of Christ, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, standing and discoursing not in a synagogue of the Jews nor in a church of Christians, but in the Areopagus of the Athenians, that is, of the most contentious and impious Greeks. For there the most talkative sects of philosophers arose. Some of these, like the very Stoics who are mentioned here, fight more over opposition of words than of things, which the apostle forbade Timothy, saying that it is useful for nothing except the subversion of the hearers. For of these, as you know, Tullius says: "For a controversy about a word has long tormented these little Greeks, more eager for contention than for truth." Yet our Paul undertook to address and correct these men, and, not frightened by the name of the place itself, which sounds of its derivation from Mars, whom they call the god of wars, there he fearlessly spoke peaceful things to those who would believe; there, girded with spiritual arms, he overthrew pernicious errors; and he feared neither the contentious, though most gentle, nor the dialecticians, though most simple.

passages.original: Haec uestri de uisibili baptismatis sacramento accipientes tantum errant, ut res absurdissimas fateri cogantur inuiti, quod ad illum scilicet fontem, qui proprius unicae columbae, de quo dictum est: nemo alienus communicet tibi, ad hortum conclusum puteumque signatum potuerit accedere Simon magus, quem legimus a Philippo baptizatum, potuerint accedere tot ficti, de quibus gemens loquitur Cyprianus: saeculo uerbis solis et non factis renuntiantes, tot episcopi auari, de quibus idem ipse testatur: fundos insidiosis fraudibus rapientes, usuris multiplicantibus faenus augentes. isti quippe baptizati et baptizantes uisibili baptismo repperiuntur: ad illum tamen fontem proprium.
passages.english: Your people, taking these things only of the visible sacrament of baptism, err so greatly that they are forced against their will to admit utterly absurd things: namely that to that fountain which is proper to the one dove, of which it was said, "Let no stranger share with you," to the enclosed garden and the sealed well, Simon Magus could have come, whom we read was baptized by Philip; that so many pretenders could have come, of whom Cyprian speaks with groaning, "renouncing the world by words alone and not by deeds"; so many avaricious bishops, of whom the same man testifies, "seizing estates by treacherous frauds, increasing interest by multiplying usury." For these are found to have been baptized and to baptize with visible baptism; yet to that proper fountain
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; continued in the following context.

passages.original: Unde, ne longum faciam, ex hac ipsa epistula ad lubaianum adtende quid ingeram, quod uestrum euertat et absumat errorem. cum enim persuadere conaretur uel sanctus Cyprianus uel quicumque illam scripsit epistulam haereticos ad ecclesiam uenientes baptizari oportere, quod uidelicet baptismus nullus deputandus esset, quem foris apud haereticos accepissent, opposuit sibi quaestionem et ait: sed dicet aliquis: quid ergo fiet de his qui in praeteritum de haeresi ad ecclesiam uenientes sine baptismo admissi sunt?
passages.english: Hence, not to be lengthy, consider what I bring forward from this very letter to Jubaianus, which overturns and consumes your error. For when either holy Cyprian or whoever wrote that letter was trying to persuade that heretics coming to the church ought to be baptized, since evidently no baptism should be counted which they had received outside among heretics, he put a question to himself and said: "But someone will say: what then will become of those who in the past, coming from heresy to the church, were admitted without baptism?"

passages.original: uides audis sentis capis intellegis, quanto scelere propter eos, qui uobis siue recte siue cum fallimini displicent, separemini ab ecclesia quae toto orbe diffunditur, cui secundum scripturas diuinas tam magnum, tam firmum, tam clarum atque luculentum testimonium perhibet Cyprianus.
passages.english: You see, hear, feel, grasp, understand with how great a crime, on account of those who displease you, whether rightly or when you are mistaken, you separate yourselves from the church which is spread throughout the whole world, to which, in accordance with the divine scriptures, Cyprian bears so great, so firm, so clear and luminous a testimony.

passages.original: si recte in ecclesiam recipiuntur ex haereticis uenientes, ut in eis error proprius corrigatur, diuinum autem sacramentum non rescindatur, bene illic uiuentibus tamquam frumentis dominicis gratulamur. si autem, sicut putatis et Cyprianum uobis in hac sententia fauere iactatis, non habent baptismum, certe admissi simpliciter ad ecclesiam secundum eundem Cyprianum propter meritum ipsius unitatis indulgentiam dei merentur nec ab ecclesiae muneribus separantur.
passages.english: If those coming from the heretics are rightly received into the church, so that their own error is corrected in them but the divine sacrament is not annulled, we rejoice over those living well there as over the Lord's grain. But if, as you think, and boast that Cyprian supports you in this opinion, they do not have baptism, certainly, according to the same Cyprian, those simply admitted to the church merit God's pardon on account of the merit of unity itself and are not separated from the gifts of the church.

passages.original: si nocentes fuerunt, non debuerunt propter illa zizania frumenta deseri, quibus nihil offuerunt. accusa quantum potes. uinco si non probas, uinco si probas; uinco, inquam, si non probas iudice te ipso, uinco si probas teste Cypriano. quid eos uis fuisse? si innocentes, cur frumentis dominicis, cum sitis zizania, calumniamini? si nocentes, cur a frumentis dominicis propter zizania separamini? exstat ecclesia cunctis clara atque conspicua, quippe ciuitas quae abscondi non potest super montem constituta, per quam dominatur Christus a mari usque ad mare et a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terrae, tamquam semen Abrahae, multiplicatum sicut stellae caeli et sicut arena maris, in quo benedicuntur omnes gentes.
passages.english: If they were guilty, the grain, which they did not harm at all, ought not to have been deserted on account of those tares. Accuse as much as you can. I win if you do not prove it, I win if you prove it; I win, I say, if you do not prove it, with you yourself as judge; I win if you prove it, with Cyprian as witness. What do you want them to have been? If innocent, why do you, though you are tares, slander the Lord's grain? If guilty, why do you separate yourselves from the Lord's grain on account of tares? The church stands out, clear and conspicuous to all, as a city set upon a mountain which cannot be hidden, through which Christ rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth, as the seed of Abraham, multiplied like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, in which all nations are blessed.

passages.original: Uos contagione malorum Afrorum ecclesiam perisse dicitis de orbe terrarum et in parte Donati eius reliquias remansisse tamquam in frumentis a zizaniis et palea separatis, contra Cyprianum apertissime sentientes, qui dicit nec malorum permixtione bonos perire in ecclesia nec eosdem malos posse ante tempus iudicii diuini a bonorum permixtione separari. uos itaque secundum uestrum errorem uel potius furorem accusare cogimini non solum Caecilianum et ordinatores eius, uerum etiam illas ecclesias, quas in scripturis apostolicis et canonicis pariter legimus, non solum Romanorum, quo ex Africa ordinare paucis uestris soletis episcopum, uerum etiam Corinthiorum, Galatarum, Ephesiorum, Thessalonicensium, Colossensium, Philippensium, ad quas apertissime scribit apostolus Paulus, Hierosolymitanam, quam primus apostolus Iacobus episcopatu suo rexit, Antiochensem, ubi primo appellati sunt discipuli christiani, Smyrnensem, Tbyatirenaem, Sardensem, Pergamensem, Philadelfensem, Laodicensem, ad quas est Apocalypsis apostoli Iohannis, tot alias ecclesias Ponti, Cappadociae, Asiae, Bithyniae, ad quas scribit apostolus Petrus, et quidquid aliud se Paulus ab Hierusalem usque ad Illyricum euangelio repleuisse testatur, ut taceam de aliis tam latis atque inmensis terrarum partibus, in quas ex his apostolicis laboribus et plantationibus porrecta creuit et crescit.
passages.english: You say that through the contagion of wicked Africans the church perished from the world and that its remnants remained in the party of Donatus, as in grain separated from tares and chaff, thinking most openly against Cyprian, who says that neither do the good perish in the church through mixture with the wicked, nor can those same wicked be separated from mixture with the good before the time of divine judgment. So, according to your error, or rather your madness, you are forced to accuse not only Caecilianus and those who ordained him, but also those churches which we likewise read of in the apostolic and canonical scriptures: not only that of the Romans, where you are accustomed to ordain a bishop from Africa for your few, but also those of the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Thessalonians, Colossians, Philippians, to whom the apostle Paul most plainly writes; that of Jerusalem, which the apostle James first ruled with his episcopate; that of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians; those of Smyrna, Thyatira, Sardis, Pergamum, Philadelphia, Laodicea, to which the Apocalypse of the apostle John is addressed; so many other churches of Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia, to which the apostle Peter writes; and whatever else Paul testifies he filled with the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum — not to mention other such broad and immense regions of the earth, into which, extended from these apostolic labours and plantings, it has grown and grows
passages.notes: Sentence continues into the following context ("the church").

passages.original: si se uellent propter illos, quos malos nouerant, a communione tot gentium, quibus eos ostendere non ualebant, uelut pestiferae contagionis timore separare, teneret eos non ego, non tu, non Donatus, non Caecilianus, sed ipse quem nominare ausus es . _ Cyprianus et diceret ea uerba, quae scripsit ad Maximum:
passages.english: if they had wished, on account of those whom they knew to be wicked, to separate themselves from the communion of so many nations, to whom they were unable to show them, as if from fear of a pestilential contagion, it would not be I, nor you, nor Donatus, nor Caecilianus who would hold them back, but the very man whom you have dared to name, Cyprian, and he would say those words which he wrote to Maximus:
passages.notes: The quotation is not included in the passage.

passages.original: respondent ideo eum sic loqui uoluisse, ne fortasse excommunicationis timore deterriti non auderent libere dicere quod sentirent, non quia cum eis esset in communione mansurus, si diuersa sensissent; ubi aperte dicunt Cyprianum esse mentitum. si enim dicebat: neminem iudicantes nec a iure communionis aliquem si diuersa senserit amouentes, quod eum dixisse conscripta indicant gesta concilii, et tamen, si quisquam eorum, quibus ea dicebat, diuersum sentire se ostenderet, non cum eo fuerat sacramenta Christi communicaturus, procul dubio mentiebatur, qui talia dolose, non ueraciter promittebat, quodque est in eo mendacio deterius, simplicitatem fratrum duplici corde fallebat, cum praesertim et scriberentur quae dicebantur.
passages.english: They reply that he chose to speak so for this reason: lest perhaps, deterred by fear of excommunication, they should not dare to say freely what they thought, not because he would remain in communion with them if they had thought differently. Here they openly say that Cyprian lied. For if he said, "judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion if he thinks differently," as the written acts of the council show he said, and yet, if any of those to whom he said this showed that he thought differently, he was not going to share the sacraments of Christ with him, then without doubt he was lying, promising such things deceitfully, not truthfully; and, what is worse in that lie, he was deceiving the simplicity of the brethren with a double heart, especially since what was said was also being written down.

passages.original: si enim hoc uerum, si hoc tenendum atque seruandum est, quod de baptismo tenemus atque seruamus, duo mala uestra nobis obicimus, unum quod erratis in baptismi quaestione, alterum quod uos ab eis, qui de hac re uerum sentiunt, separatis. si autem, ut secundum uos loquar, hoc est in ea quaestione uerum quod ipsi sentitis, illo certe crimine maculamini, quod ab ecclesia recessistis, propter cuius pacem, sicut Cyprianus et fecit et monuit, etiam diuersa sentientes ferre debuistis.
passages.english: For if what we hold and observe concerning baptism is true, if it is to be held and observed, we charge you with two evils of yours: one, that you err on the question of baptism; the other, that you separate yourselves from those who think the truth on this matter. But if, to speak on your terms, what you yourselves think is the truth on that question, you are certainly stained with that crime, that you have withdrawn from the church, for the sake of whose peace, as Cyprian both did and advised, you ought to have borne even those who thought differently.

passages.original: cur autem dixerim malos communionis nostrae, hoc est areae dominicae paleam, cum in uos inique agunt, a bonis nostris laudabiliter pro pace tolerari, quid opus est ut ipse ostendam, ipse defendam, cum pro me beatus Cyprianus apertissime et candidissime dicat, etiam cum cernuntur in ecclesia mali, non propter eos ecclesiam deserendam, hoc est quod dixi eos pro unitatis pace tolerandos? neque enim uos amplius quam nos persequuntur, qui uos inique persequentes dant uobis ad decipiendos imperitos licet falsam similitudinem gloriae, uobis autem uulnus grande tristitiae.
passages.english: But why I said that the wicked of our communion, that is, the chaff of the Lord's threshing floor, when they act unjustly against you, are laudably tolerated by our good members for the sake of peace, what need is there for me to show it myself, to defend it myself, when on my behalf the blessed Cyprian says most openly and most candidly that even when the wicked are seen in the church, the church is not to be deserted because of them, which is what I said, that they are to be tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity? For they do not persecute you more than they do us, they who, persecuting you unjustly, give you a semblance of glory, false though it is, for deceiving the unlearned, but to you a great wound of sorrow.

passages.original: si enim baptismus Christi est et ideo nullo modo destruendus, qui datus est per Felici anum et Praetextatum, cum separati a uobis Maximiano coniungerentur, cum illo a nobis pro nefarii schismatis crimine condemnati, quomodo non est baptismus Christi uel quomodo destruendus est, qui datur in ecclesia, quae ramos suos, ut uerbis Cypriani utar, per uniuersam terram copia ubertatis extendit, qui datur postremo in illis ecclesiis, quas numquam in litteris apostolicis recitare cessastis, numquam ullo concilio sicut Felicianum Praetextatumque damnastis? si damnatos in integrum restituere placuit pro resareienda parte Donati, quid uos offendit toto orbe diffusa unitas Christi, quae uel damnare non potuit inauditos uel omnino nec damnauit nec absoluit incognitos uel innocentes credidit quos didicit absolutos?
passages.english: For if the baptism which was given through Felicianus and Praetextatus, when, separated from you, they were joined to Maximianus, condemned with him by you for the crime of a wicked schism, is the baptism of Christ and therefore by no means to be destroyed, how is that not the baptism of Christ, or how is that to be destroyed, which is given in the church that, to use Cyprian's words, extends its branches through the whole earth in abundance of fruitfulness, which is given, finally, in those churches which you have never ceased to read out in the apostolic letters, [and] which you have never condemned in any council as you did Felicianus and Praetextatus? If it pleased [you] to restore the condemned to their full standing in order to mend the party of Donatus, what offends you in the unity of Christ spread through the whole world, which either could not condemn people unheard, or neither condemned nor acquitted at all people unknown [to it], or believed those innocent whom it learned had been acquitted?
passages.notes: "a nobis" (by us) read as "a uobis" (by you), as the sense requires; "Felici anum" and "resareienda" (resarcienda) are scanning errors.

passages.original: Sed quid ad rem, cuius inter nos uertitur quaestio, qualis ipse sim, cum in area dominica sim stipula si malus, granum si bonus? uos tamen si grana essetis, paleam conmixtam, sicut admonet etiam ipse Cyprianus, ante tempus uentilationis non refugeretis. proinde nos, si quem repperimus in nobis notum hominem malum, recte uobis obicimus; ibi enim tota defensio uestra consistit, quia propterea uos separastis, ne alienorum peccatorum contagione periretis.
passages.english: But what has it to do with the matter in question between us, what sort of man I myself am, since on the Lord's threshing floor I am straw if wicked, grain if good? Yet you, if you were grain, would not flee from the chaff mixed [with you] before the time of winnowing, as Cyprian himself also advises. Accordingly, if we find among us any known wicked man, we rightly lay it to your charge; for your whole defence rests on this, that you separated yourselves so as not to perish by the contagion of others' sins.
passages.notes: The final sentence's logic is odd as transmitted (one might expect "you rightly charge us"); translated as it stands.

passages.original: sicut nec undecim apostoli furtis Iudae communicabant et tamen cum illo eidem domino uisibiliter cohaerebant, eundem magistrum audiebant, idem credendum euangelium percipiebant, eadem sacramenta sumebant, corporali cum illo congregatione permixti, spiritali dissimilitudine separati; sicut apostolus Paulus non communicabat contumaciae et inuidiae, hoc est diabolicis uitiis eorum, qui non caste Christum adnuntiabant, et tamen cum eis eundem Christum praedicabat, eiusdem Christi sacramenta participabat et de his dicebat: siue occasione siue ueritate Christus adnuntietur - nam hos martyr Cyprianus amantissimus unitatis non aliquo schismate uel haerese separatos, sed fratribus corporali congregatione fuisse commixtos et intellexit et scripsit —; sicut idem ipse Cyprianus auaritiae rapinis faenori collegarum non communicabat, quos dicebat e sur i en t i bus in ecclesia fratribus habere argentum largiter uelle, fundos insidiosis fraudibus rapere, usuris multiplicantibus faenus augere, quod malum etiam idololatriae conparauit, quorum tamen corporalem congregationem non refugiebat, ad eadem altaria consistebat, eundem sacratissimum cibum potumque sumebat. illi enim non aliis, sed sibi iudicium manducabant et bibebant, ille autem cum talibus non eorum peccata, sed mysteria Christi communicabat, coniunctissimus coetibus, disiunctissimus moribus.
passages.english: just as the eleven apostles did not share in the thefts of Judas and yet visibly adhered with him to the same Lord, heard the same master, received the same gospel to be believed, took the same sacraments, mingled with him in bodily assembly, separated by spiritual unlikeness; just as the apostle Paul did not share in the obstinacy and envy, that is, the devilish vices, of those who did not proclaim Christ purely, and yet preached the same Christ with them, partook of the sacraments of the same Christ, and said of them: "whether in pretence or in truth, let Christ be proclaimed" (for the martyr Cyprian, the great lover of unity, both understood and wrote that these were not separated by any schism or heresy but mingled with the brethren in bodily assembly); just as the same Cyprian himself did not share in the greed, the plunder and the usury of his colleagues, who, he said, while brethren in the church were starving, wanted to hold silver in abundance, to seize estates by treacherous frauds, to increase their interest by multiplying usuries, an evil which he even compared to idolatry, yet he did not flee their bodily assembly, stood at the same altars, took the same most sacred food and drink. For they ate and drank judgement not to others but to themselves, while he shared with such men not their sins but the mysteries of Christ, most closely joined in assemblies, most widely separated in morals.
passages.notes: "e sur i en t i bus" read as esurientibus.

passages.original: si autem hoc tam maiori numero collegarum et tot suae communionis ecclesiis per totam Africam diffusis persuadere non possent, aut sententiam suam consilio saniore rescinderent, in qua falli sicut homines de homine potuerunt, aut, si uera eius crimina sine ulla dubitatione didicerant, quae tamen persuadere tanto pluribus ceteris non ualebant, nocentem scientes tolerarent prudentius et patientius, quam se a tot innocentibus. qui ista nescirent, impio schismate separarent. tenerent enim illam beati Cypriani plenissimam caritatis pietatisque sententiam, qua dicit: nam etsi uidentur in ecclesia esse zizania, non tamen impediri debet fides aut caritas nostra, ut quoniam zizania esse in ecclesia cernimus ipsi de ecclesia recedamus. quod quidem illis tono prodesset, si in ecclesiae catholicae gremio purgati purgamenta tolerarent, quae ante tempus separare non possent. sed quod eos dicimus in hac erroris uestri societate, quam ueram ecclesiam esse arbitramini, facere debuisse, hoc maiores uestri in illa perspicue uera, in cuius unitate fuerunt, ne ab illa separarentur, facere debuerunt.
passages.english: But if they could not persuade so much larger a number of colleagues and so many churches of their communion spread through all Africa of this, they should either have rescinded their sentence on wiser counsel, a sentence in which they could have been deceived, as men about a man, or, if they had learned his true crimes beyond any doubt, which nevertheless they could not persuade so many more others of, they should, knowing him guilty, have tolerated him with more prudence and patience than separate themselves by impious schism from so many innocent men who did not know these things. For they would have held to that sentence of blessed Cyprian, most full of charity and piety, in which he says: "For even if there seem to be tares in the church, our faith or charity ought not to be hindered, so that, because we see there are tares in the church, we ourselves withdraw from the church." This would indeed have profited them greatly, if, cleansed within the bosom of the catholic church, they had tolerated the refuse which they could not separate before the time. But what we say they ought to have done in this society of your error, which you think to be the true church, your forebears ought to have done in that clearly true one, in whose unity they were, so as not to be separated from it.

passages.original: et hinc eminet eos a uobis exisse, non uos ab ipsis, quia uos etiam in his terris estis ubi ipsi sunt, illi autem, quaquauersus uos estis, non nisi forte peregrinantes inueniuntur —, sic ecclesia catholica, quae, sicut ait Cyprianus, ramos suos per uniuersam terram copia ubertatis extendit, ubique sustinet scandala eorum, qui ab illa uitio maxime superbiae praeciduntur, aliorum hic, aliorum alibi atque alibi, qui partes suas ostentantes dicunt: ecce hic est Christus, ecce illic, quibus ne credatur ipse praemonuit. non enim ostendunt uiam, de qua prophetatum est in psalmis: ut cognoscamus in terra uiam tuam, in omnibus gentibus salutare tuum, sed suae communionis quisque regiones, ecce hic, ecce illic. ubi enim cadunt, ibi remanent, et ubi separantur, ibi arescunt. unde ipsa de qua praeciduntur etiam in eas terras extenditur, ubi iacent illa in sua quaeque regione fragmenta;
passages.english: and hence it stands out that they went out from you, not you from them, because you are also in those lands where they are, whereas they, wherever you are, are not found except perhaps as travellers — so the catholic church, which, as Cyprian says, extends its branches through the whole earth in abundance of fruitfulness, everywhere endures the offences of those who are cut off from it chiefly by the vice of pride, some here, others elsewhere and elsewhere, who, displaying their parties, say: "Look, here is Christ; look, there," whom he himself warned beforehand not to be believed. For they do not show the way of which it was prophesied in the psalms: "that we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations," but each the regions of his own communion: "look here, look there." For where they fall, there they remain, and where they are separated, there they wither. Hence the very [church] from which they are cut off extends even into those lands where those fragments lie, each in its own region;
